examples.title: Transport: public services or roads?
examples.task_prompt: Some people believe that governments should spend more money on public transport than on building new roads. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
examples.essay:
Cities have limited budgets, so transport spending requires clear priorities. Although new roads can be necessary in growing areas, I believe that governments should generally invest more in public transport because it moves people efficiently and gives more residents access to essential services.

The main advantage of public transport is its ability to carry large numbers of passengers without requiring each person to drive. A frequent bus service or a reliable railway can reduce pressure on busy routes during the morning rush. By contrast, a wider road may encourage additional car journeys, so the initial improvement can disappear as traffic grows. Public investment is therefore more useful when it offers a practical alternative to driving rather than simply creating extra space for cars.

A second reason concerns access. Students, older people and workers on low incomes may not own a car. If their neighbourhood has no dependable bus connection, they can struggle to reach colleges, hospitals or suitable jobs. Affordable fares and services that run outside office hours can make a considerable difference. However, buying new vehicles alone is insufficient: governments must also fund maintenance, accessible stops and a timetable that people can trust.

This does not mean that road construction should stop. Rural communities still need safe roads, and some missing connections prevent buses and emergency vehicles from operating effectively. Such projects should be judged by their practical value rather than the assumption that every traffic problem requires another lane.

Overall, public transport deserves the larger share of investment in most urban settings. Targeted road improvements remain useful, but a dependable transport network provides broader benefits than expanding road capacity alone.

examples.title: Education: homework every day?
examples.task_prompt: Some people think that schoolchildren should receive homework every day, while others believe that they should have more free time after school. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
examples.essay:
Homework is a normal part of school life, but families disagree about how much children should receive. Some believe daily homework builds good habits, while others worry that it leaves too little time for rest and interests. In my opinion, homework can be useful, but it should have a clear purpose and should not be given every day automatically.

People who support daily homework argue that practice helps children remember what they learn. For example, a short mathematics exercise can show whether a pupil understands a method without help from the teacher. Regular tasks may also encourage children to organise their time and take responsibility for their work. Teachers can use these exercises to identify difficulties before the next lesson. These benefits are strongest when a task is short and closely connected to classroom learning.

On the other hand, children already spend many hours following instructions at school. They need opportunities to play, exercise and speak with their families. If homework fills the whole evening, they may become tired and complete it without thinking carefully. Home conditions are also different. One child may have a quiet room and support from a parent, while another shares a crowded room and has nobody available to explain the task. A large amount of homework can make these differences more important.

I would therefore prefer a flexible approach. Teachers should give practice when it helps a particular learning goal, while allowing homework-free evenings for other activities. Schools should also coordinate the tasks set by different subjects so that several deadlines do not arrive together.

To conclude, daily practice has advantages, but the amount of homework matters less than its value. Carefully chosen tasks and sufficient free time can support learning together.

examples.title: Work: working from home
examples.task_prompt: More employees are now working from home instead of travelling to an office. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?
examples.essay:
Working from home has become possible for many office employees because meetings and documents can be shared online. This development creates difficulties for communication and personal boundaries, but I think its advantages are greater when employers organise remote work carefully.

One important benefit is the time saved by avoiding a daily commute. An employee who previously travelled for an hour each way can use some of that time for sleep, exercise or family responsibilities. This can make a normal working day less exhausting. Companies may benefit as well, since they can recruit people who live outside the area around their office. For a small business looking for a specialist, a wider choice of applicants can be particularly valuable.

However, home working is not equally suitable for everyone. Some employees have limited space or share their home with people whose routines are different. Online communication can also make a simple question take longer to resolve, especially when colleagues work at different times. New staff may miss the informal conversations that help them understand how a team operates. These disadvantages can reduce the value of working remotely if managers assume that providing a laptop is enough.

The most serious problem is that work can continue into personal time. Without a clear finishing point, employees may feel that they must answer messages throughout the evening. Employers should set reasonable expectations about availability and provide regular opportunities for direct discussion. Occasional office days may also help teams maintain relationships, although the arrangement should reflect the actual work rather than a fixed rule for every job.

In conclusion, remote work offers substantial benefits through flexibility and reduced travel. Its disadvantages are real, but many can be managed through suitable equipment, clear working hours and deliberate communication.
